deep.reconstruction:
The heading reads 'Periodorum quas servant fractiones communes per decimales expressae tabula': a table of the periods of ordinary fractions written as decimals. For each prime p from 3 to 137, Gauss writes every distinct repetend (period) of the fractions r/p (1 <= r < p).

(1) Underlying theory, in modern terms. Let e = ord_p(10). Then every r/p has a purely periodic expansion of period length e. The period of r/p is the integer r*(10^e-1)/p, padded to e digits. Multiplying r by 10 cyclically rotates its period. So fractions whose numerators lie in the same coset r*<10> of (Z/pZ)^* share one cyclic period. The number of distinct periods is therefore (p-1)/e.

(2) The data. Primes for which 10 is a primitive root get one period of length p-1: 7, 17, 19, 23, 29, 47, 59, 61, 97, 109, 113, 131. The other primes get several periods:
- 13: e=6, 2 periods
- 31: e=15, 2 periods
- 37: e=3, 12 periods
- 41: e=5, 8 periods
- 43: e=21, 2 periods
- 53: e=13, 4 periods
- 67: e=33, 2 periods
- 71: e=35, 2 periods
- 73: e=8, 9 periods
- 79: e=13, 6 periods
- 83: e=41, 2 periods
- 89: e=44, 2 periods
- 101: e=4, 25 periods
- 103: e=34, 3 periods
- 107: e=53, 2 periods
- 127: e=42, 3 periods
- 137: e=8, 17 periods

The 1/p period is written cyclically shifted by one place: the first digit (for p > 10 the leading 0) goes to the end, i.e. the period of 10/p.
- 1/17 = 0.(0588235294117647) is entered as 5882352941176470.
- 1/103 = 0.(0097...2233) is entered as 0970873786...2330.
- 3/7 gives 428571, which is 10/7 mod 1.

Identifications of the other periods (my checks):
- 13: 615384 = 8/13, 769230 = 10/13.
- 31: 483870967741935 = 15/31.
- 43: 511627906976744186046 = 22/43.
- 53: 48, 29, 12 over 53.
- 67: 53/67.
- 71: 52/71.
- 79: 53, 17, 77, 36, 19 over 79.
- 83: 2/83.
- 89: 33/89.
- 103: 60/103 and 51/103.
- 107: 95/107.
- 127: 44/127 and 92/127.

(3) Arrangement and probable method of computation (my reconstruction, verified on several primes). When a prime has many periods, the numerators along the listing form a geometric progression r_{k+1} = m*r_k mod p, ending with the shifted 1/p period. Here m is a fixed generator of the quotient group (Z/p)^*/<10>.
- p=101: read down the columns, the entries are 1980, 3960, 7920, 5841, 1683, 3366, ... Each is double the previous modulo 9999, i.e. numerators 20*2^k mod 101. The chain closes at 4950 -> 9900, which is in the class of 0990 = 10/101.
- p=137: numerators 120, 70, 18, 79, 126, 5, 60, 35, 9, 108, 63, 71, 30, 86, 73, 54, then 10. This is multiplication by 12 each step; each period is that numerator times 729927 = (10^8-1)/137.
- p=73: numerators 50, 31, 9, 45, 6, 30, 4, 20, 10, multiplication by 5 (with a rotation at the end).
- p=41: read down the columns, numerators 19, 32, 28, 4, 24, 21, 3, 10; multiplication by 6, a primitive root.
- p=37: read down the columns, numerators 13, 28, 29, 34, 22, 36, 32, 12, 23, 4, 20, 10; multiplication by 5, i.e. by 10/2.

So each period was almost certainly produced from its neighbour by multiplying the digit string by a small number (doubling, etc.) modulo 10^e-1, then rotating. This orders the periods by index with respect to a primitive root, exactly as Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312-318 require for converting any a/p by means of indices.

(4) Purpose. This is the working table behind DA art. 316-318 and Gauss's later 'Tafel zur Verwandlung gemeiner Brüche in Decimalbrüche' (Werke II). Together with an index table, it lets one write down the decimal expansion of any fraction with prime denominator at once.
errors: p=59: the transcribed last group '6779661016' would make 60 digits; the period of 10/59 has 58 digits and must end '...6271186440 67796610'. This is either a transcription error or a slip; the image shows an 8-digit group, probably '67796610'.
p=103: a crossed-out false start '7475728155' (a rotation of the first period 60/103 = ...7475728155...) precedes the second period 4951456310... It was correctly cancelled.
p=107: in '8224299065' the final digit is overwritten 5/6; the correct digit is 5 (95/107 = 0.8878504672 8971962616 8224299065...).
p=127: the first row has a cancelled tail after '28'. The second row '5275590551' shows overwriting. The printed values 44/127 and 92/127 are correct as transcribed.
p=101: corrections at 4950 / 0990. The doubling chain 4950 -> 9900 lands in the class of 1/101, which is represented in the table as 0990 = 10/101. This is consistent.
Entries for 3 and 11 are anomalous or unclear: '6' for 3 is 2/3, not the shifted 1/3. The '31(?)' beside 11 does not match any period of r/11 (09, 18, 27, 36, 45, ...) and is probably a misreading.

results.what: Complete list of distinct decimal periods of r/p for all primes p <= 137, grouped by cosets of <10> in (Z/p)^*, each period of length ord_p(10)
results.modern_name: Repetends of 1/p; cyclic numbers; cosets of the subgroup generated by 10 in (Z/pZ)^*
results.usually_credited_to: Periodic decimals studied by Wallis, Lambert, Robertson, J. Bernoulli; large tables by Henry Goodwyn (1818-23) and Burckhardt; theory systematized by Gauss, DA arts. 312-318 (1801)

results.what: Computing successive periods by multiplying the previous period by a fixed generator of (Z/p)^*/<10> (e.g. doubling for p=101, x12 for p=137, x5 for p=73), ordered by index
results.modern_name: Using the cyclic structure of the quotient group (Z/p)^*/<10> (index/discrete-log arrangement) to generate all repetends
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 316-317, and his posthumously published decimal-conversion table (Werke II, 1863)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript draft of Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods for prime denominators, described in DA arts. 312-318 and published in Werke II. The construction by successive multiplication by a quotient-group generator is a nice detail but fully consistent with his published method.
